name: Zoe Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that doesn't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greenbank, which is a farming co-op, so about thirty members own it and a dozen of us actually work it. We grow vegetables for a box scheme, leeks, squash, potatoes, and we run about two hundred sheep on the hill. My day is weeding, picking, packing boxes on Tuesdays and Fridays, and helping with the flock when they need hands. I joined two years ago after the bakery I worked at for fifteen years closed, so I'm still the one who plants the onions upside down.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Once, and they've never let me forget it. What I love is that we vote on things, I get the same say as people who've farmed for decades. What wears me out is my back and the money, because a co-op pays fairly but not much, and Dev's school bus wages don't stretch either. We've got Maya, who's fourteen, and Arun, who's ten, and the mortgage, and maybe two weeks of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of fuss over a fancy spell-checker. At the co-op meeting I'd probably say thank goodness, now can we talk about the irrigation pump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means my life carries on, which is fine. I don't need the world to change, I need the leeks to come up and the boxes to sell. The money's tight, but that's not AI's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the weather app for spray days, which I do already. Maybe I'd ask the co-op again about a tractor course so I can drive the bigger one. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit of relief that one thing on the list of worries can be crossed off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money's tight but not AI's fault. Whose fault is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Supermarkets, mostly. They set what food is worth and it's never enough for the people growing it. That's why I like the box scheme, the money comes straight to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the tractor course change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a pound an hour more and a lot less weeding by hand. Kev, who runs the field crew, says I'm ready, I just need the certificate. My knees would thank me.

S0.say: She'd say AI was a lot of fuss over a fancy spell-checker. At the co-op meeting she'd move straight on to practical matters like the irrigation pump.
S0.think: Privately she thinks a plateau leaves her life as it is, which suits her. Her money worries come from supermarket prices, not technology.
S0.do: Keeps working as before and keeps using a weather app to plan spray days. Asks the co-op again to fund a tractor course, worth about a pound an hour more.
S0.feel: Calm, with some relief that one worry is gone.
S0.quote: I don't need the world to change, I need the leeks to come up and the boxes to sell.
S0.fieldNote: Her worries are about money and her body, and she places the blame for low pay on supermarkets. The co-op's voting gives her a sense of agency that a hired hand might not have. She uses simple tech practically without much interest in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the co-op straight out, that if we bring in machines, the members decide how and nobody gets dumped. Online I'd share stuff about worker-owned farms and how they handle this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think weeding robots come for my job first. They're already on the bigger veg farms, little things that crawl the rows with a camera. I'm the one doing exactly that by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the co-op to put a robot weeder on the agenda early, so we choose it and plan who does what instead. I'd volunteer to learn how it works, because I'd rather run it than be replaced by it. I'd also start using the chatbot more, Maya showed me how to ask it about pests and it's not bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared, because we'd decide it together. If I were a hired hand on a big farm I'd feel very different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the members voted for the robot and fewer hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to live with it, that's what voting means. But I've known these people two years and I don't think they'd do it cold. We're the kind of place that argues for three meetings about the price of a cabbage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather run it than be replaced by it. Do you think you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once someone shows me, yes. I'm not first to anything, I waited a year before I trusted the weather app. But once I see it working I'm stubborn about learning it properly.

S1.say: She'd tell the co-op that if machines come in, members decide how and nobody gets dumped. Online she'd share examples of worker-owned farms handling the change.
S1.think: Privately she expects robot weeders to target her job first, since hand weeding is most of what she does. She trusts the co-op's slow decision-making to soften it.
S1.do: Asks the co-op to put a robot weeder on the agenda early and volunteers to learn to run one. Uses a chatbot more often for pest questions, as her daughter showed her.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not scared, because the decision would be shared.
S1.quote: We're the kind of place that argues for three meetings about the price of a cabbage.
S1.fieldNote: Ownership changes how she sees risk: the same machine feels less threatening when members vote on it. She is a steady adopter who waits to see things work and then commits. Her daughter is her route into new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs public money for ordinary people, right now, an income for everyone while it shakes out. I'd be writing to our representative and getting the co-op to sign a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the co-op might not survive. If a big farm with robots can grow leeks for half our price, our box customers love us but they'll still look at their bank balance. And Dev drives a bus, which is exactly the kind of thing that'll drive itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month I'd sit down with Dev and go through every bill, and cut anything that isn't food, house or heat. I'd sign up for any public support the day it exists. I'd push the co-op to buy a robot ourselves, together, instead of being beaten by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightening. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Both your jobs at once. What does that look like at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like the two of us with a calculator and a pot of tea gone cold. We've got about two weeks of bills saved. If both of us lose work in the same year, that's not a crisis, that's the end of the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes away the steady part of me. Normally I wait to see if a thing works, but with two years there's no waiting, by the time it's proven it's already happened. So I'd have to jump before I'm ready, and I hate that.

S2.say: She'd call loudly for public money for ordinary people, like an income for everyone during the change. She'd write to her representative and get the co-op to sign a letter.
S2.think: Privately she fears the co-op couldn't compete on price with robot-run farms, and that her partner's bus job would go too. Two jobs lost at once would mean losing the house.
S2.do: Goes through every bill with her partner in the first month and cuts anything beyond food, housing and heat. Signs up for public support as soon as it exists and pushes the co-op to buy a robot together.
S2.quote: If both of us lose work in the same year, that's not a crisis, that's the end of the house.
S2.fieldNote: The household's double exposure, farm work and bus driving, is what turns this from worry to alarm. She notices that two years takes away her normal habit of waiting until something is proven. Her instinct is still collective: buy the robot together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so let's not waste it. I'd want the co-op and other small farms to band together and share machines and skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is probably just enough for me. I'd be forty-eight. If I learn the robot side in the first two years, I might be the one keeping our machines running in year five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the co-op to pay for me to do a farm machinery maintenance course at the college in the evenings. I'd try to save thirty a week, which means no holiday for a couple of years. And I'd tell Dev to look at getting a mechanic's ticket while there's still time, maybe on the buses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but busy, which is better than anxious and stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does no holiday mean for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the week at my sister's by the sea doesn't happen, and the kids will moan about it. Arun counts down to it from Easter. But I'd rather have that row than the other one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even if you keep the machines running, AGI does that too in the end. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, I'm not daft. The plan isn't to beat the robot forever, it's to still be standing when the rules finally catch up. By year five I'm hoping the government has done something, and I'd want to be in work when it does.

S3.say: She'd say five years is a warning that shouldn't be wasted. She'd want small farms to band together and share machines and skills.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years is just enough for her to learn the robot side and keep the co-op's machines running. She knows that only buys time until the rules catch up.
S3.do: Asks the co-op to fund an evening machinery maintenance course and saves thirty a week by skipping holidays. Urges her partner to train as a mechanic while there's still time.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, which she prefers to anxious and stuck.
S3.quote: The plan isn't to beat the robot forever, it's to still be standing when the rules finally catch up.
S3.fieldNote: With a few years' warning her steady style becomes a plan: learn, save, and wait for policy. She is clear-eyed that AGI eventually does maintenance too. Her goal is to bridge to whatever public support arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly if anyone in charge has the nerve. Farms like ours should get help to own the machines, not just the big boys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. Maya would be through school, Arun nearly, and the co-op has time to change shape. I might not be weeding but I think I'd still be at Greenbank doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the machinery course over two or three years, steadily, not panicking. I'd push the co-op to apply for any grant for shared robots. And I'd keep using the AI stuff a bit more each year, once I've seen others get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly I'd feel there's time to turn round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Maya about choosing what to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To pick something with people in it. Nursing, teaching, something where you'd want a person in the room. She wants to be a vet, and honestly I'd back that, animals need hands and judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years feels manageable. What would make it not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big companies buy up all the land in those ten years. The robots I can live with. It's who owns them that keeps me up. If the co-op got priced out of our own fields, that would undo everything.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough to handle the change fairly if leaders have the nerve. Small farms like hers should get help to own machines too.
S4.think: Privately she finds ten years manageable, with her children grown and time for the co-op to change. She expects to still be at Greenbank in some role.
S4.do: Takes the machinery course over two or three years and pushes the co-op to apply for grants for shared robots. Uses AI tools a bit more each year as others prove them.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly feels there's time to turn round.
S4.quote: The robots I can live with. It's who owns them that keeps me up.
S4.fieldNote: Her real fear in the long picture is ownership, not the machines themselves. She would steer her daughter towards work with people or animals. The decade suits her steady, wait-and-prove approach.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of Dev and me both being hit at once. What would help is an income floor while people retrain, and grants so co-ops can buy machines together. Give the small places a fair chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the co-op means to people. It's not just a job, it's where I found my feet after the bakery. When the bakery closed I lost a job; if Greenbank closed I'd lose the people I argue with every Thursday.

headlineQuote: When the bakery closed I lost a job; if Greenbank closed I'd lose the people I argue with every Thursday.
portrait: Zoe Gupta is a 43-year-old junior worker at Greenbank, a farming co-op that grows box-scheme vegetables and keeps sheep. She joined after her bakery closed, lives with her partner Dev, a school bus driver, and their two children, and has about two weeks of bills saved. She blames supermarkets for low farm pay and trusts the co-op's slow, voting way of deciding things. She is calm in the plateau, uneasy with steady change, alarmed by two-year AGI because both household jobs are exposed, and steadier with more time, planning a machinery course. Her deepest worry is who will own the robots.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because she and her bus-driver partner could lose work in the same year and lose the house.
whatWouldHelp: An income floor while people retrain, and grants so co-ops and small farms can buy machines together.
